Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

Data Storage & External Services

Both web applications are configured for SQL Server LocalDB and keep product pictures in application files. The legacy application uses EF6 and the ported application uses EF Core. No message broker, remote application API, or distributed cache was identified; Application Insights is the only external telemetry integration evidenced in the legacy project.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The solution keeps the original MVC application and a separately packaged port side by side rather than splitting the catalog into independently deployed services.
  • Autofac selects either a mock catalog service or a database-backed service from an application setting.
  • The two web projects have independent persistence contexts and configuration; their deployment-time data sharing is not established by the source.

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType are service-level domain entities used in MVC views and API responses. The legacy /api/files endpoint returns a binary-serialized list of BrandDTO values; the DTO contains Id and Brand. The utility exposes BinaryFormatter serialization and deserialization. No OpenAPI, protobuf, or GraphQL contract files were found. JSON contracts are framework defaults plus Newtonsoft.Json references; the source does not establish a custom serialization policy.

Communication Patterns

Requests use synchronous HTTP between browser/API clients and the selected application. Controllers call ICatalogService directly; database-backed implementations call EF6 or EF Core, while mock mode uses an in-memory implementation. No queue, service discovery, gateway aggregation, retry policy, circuit breaker, or cross-service client was identified.

The legacy MVC create/edit/delete actions include anti-forgery validation. No authentication or role-based authorization configuration was identified. The ported launch profile supports local HTTPS, but the source does not demonstrate TLS enforcement for deployed traffic.

Core Business Workflows

The applications support browsing and maintaining a product catalog. They expose catalog items with brand and type associations, but no order, payment, or customer workflows were identified.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogA product offered in the catalog, with price and stock informationBelongs to one brand and one type
CatalogBrandCatalogA brand used to group catalog productsHas many catalog items
CatalogTypeCatalogA product classificationHas many catalog items

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server in database-backed mode; local picture files
eShopPortedCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server in database-backed mode; static picture files
eShopLegacy.UtilitiesShared infrastructureNoneUsed for binary serialization by files endpoints

The two web applications implement their own catalog service and persistence context. No cross-context API calls, event exchange, or shared aggregation workflow was found.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse Catalog

  1. A visitor opens the catalog index, optionally supplying page size and page index.
  2. The controller asks ICatalogService for a page of catalog items.
  3. The database-backed service counts and loads items ordered by identifier, including each item's brand and type; mock mode reads the in-memory list.
  4. The controller populates picture URIs and renders the catalog view.

Workflow 2: Create a Catalog Item

  1. An operator submits the create form with a CatalogItem and anti-forgery token.
  2. MVC model validation checks the submitted model. Invalid submissions return the form with validation errors.
  3. The service obtains an identifier from the Hi/Lo generator, adds the item, and saves it; mock mode updates its in-memory collection.
  4. On success, the controller redirects to the catalog index.

Workflow 3: Edit or Delete a Catalog Item

The edit flow loads the selected item, validates the submitted model and then saves the modified catalog record. The delete flow resolves the item by identifier and removes it. Both return to the catalog index on completion.

Cross-Service Data Flows

No cross-service data composition or fallback between independently deployed services was found. Each application serves its own catalog operations and accesses its own service/context. The BrandsController delete routes validate that a brand exists but are demonstrative and do not actually delete it.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant Operator participant Controller as "Catalog Controller" participant Service as "Catalog Service" participant Generator as "HiLo Generator" participant Context as "Catalog Context" participant Database as "SQL Server" Operator->>Controller: Submit new catalog item Controller->>Controller: Validate model and anti-forgery token alt Valid item Controller->>Service: Create catalog item Service->>Generator: Request identifier Generator->>Database: Read SQL sequence when needed Database-->>Generator: Sequence block Generator-->>Service: Assigned identifier Service->>Context: Add item and save Context->>Database: Insert catalog record Database-->>Context: Save result Context-->>Service: Completion Service-->>Controller: Completion Controller-->>Operator: Redirect to catalog index else Invalid item Controller-->>Operator: Return form with validation feedback end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog items require a name; price has a numeric format and range of 0 through 1,000,000.
  • Available stock, restock threshold, and maximum stock threshold each have a configured range of 0 through 10,000,000.
  • The persistence model requires each catalog item to reference an existing brand and type.
  • The legacy database-backed service allocates identifiers from SQL sequence blocks; the mock service assigns the next value from its current list.
  • Create and edit MVC actions use anti-forgery validation. No business-role authorization or audit trail was identified.
  • Each database write calls EF SaveChanges; no explicit cross-operation transaction or compensating workflow was found.

Dependency Map

The solution declares external packages for its two web projects. After duplicate declarations in the legacy project file and packages.config are collapsed, the projects contain approximately 59 unique package/version coordinates; the shared utility project uses framework references.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The solution targets .NET Framework 4.7.2 and 4.6.1 and includes ASP.NET Core 2.2, EF Core 2.2, MVC 5, and EF6 packages. These are legacy stacks requiring substantial compatibility work for a current .NET target. The CVE scan found medium-severity log4net and high-severity Newtonsoft.Json advisories for the affected declared versions; see the security assessment for affected locations and ranges.

Notable Observations

  • The legacy MVC project contains both PackageReference declarations and packages.config entries; duplicate package declarations were collapsed for this summary.
  • The two applications declare different versions of Autofac and Newtonsoft.Json.
  • No test-scoped packages or test projects were detected in the assessed solution.
  • Package dependency-tree resolution could not run because the legacy Web Application targets are absent from the installed .NET SDK; this inventory uses direct project declarations and packages.config, not transitive resolution.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The catalog domain is persisted by SQL Server through two separate persistence implementations: EF6 in the legacy application and EF Core in the ported application. Both define the same core entities: catalog items, brands, and types.

The legacy initializer seeds catalog records and uses SQL sequence scripts for Hi/Lo identifiers. The ported project applies EF Core entity configuration from its assembly.

Caching Strategy

No distributed or application cache provider was identified. Mock mode stores records in an in-memory list for the process lifetime; this is the mock data source, not a configured cache.

Data Ownership Boundaries

Each web application owns its catalog context and persistence code. There is no separate catalog service or database-per-domain boundary in the solution. Source configuration points both projects at local SQL Server development databases, but does not establish that deployed instances share one database. Controllers call their own catalog service; cross-application data access through APIs or messaging was not found. The legacy service uses sequence allocation for new identifiers; no CQRS or outbox pattern was identified.
